content: Discussion for #Project announcements > Lean Pool -- arXiv-like Lean library @ 💬

I saw MOTIVATION.md but I still don't understand how this differs from merely-true. IIUC the plan for merely-true includes everything in that document (even though it isn't all implemented yet).

Although, the more the merrier :)

Since it mentions "formalizations get maintained", I assume you're planning to run agents on the repo (maybe with Hopscotch?).
So as a human, is it in scope for me to PR a bunch of proof_wanteds to have these agents fill them in?
Something like #general > theorems.fun - bounty platform for Lean theorems and #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Proof Flow Aristotle

I still don't understand how this differs from merely-true

Two answers:

  1. merely-true does not seem to be maintained or active. I tried to revive it but without success.
  2. merely-true is exactly what it sounds like -- it's merely true. I can make a 100k LOC PR with lemmas like 1+1=2 or a PR with theorem FermatLastTheorem : True := True.intro or a PR with set_option maxHeartbeats 9999999999 in ... that will take hours or days to compile, and all of these PRs will get merged because they are (merely) true. Also, merely-true does not bump projects - it just drops them, so each mathlib bump is essentially a complete reset. Also, merely-true does not build docs. Also, it does not do any data provenance.

I think there is a middle-ground between mathlib and merely-true, just like there is a middle ground between top-end math journals and viXra (arXiv is that middle groud). Whether Lean Pool is this middle ground - time will tell.

I assume you're planning to run agents on the repo

Yes, I've sunk over 1000 agent hours into the repo already. The CI and LLM reviewer are very strict, so it takes considerable effort to bring an old unmaintained one-off formalization up to Lean Pool's quality (which is, of course, far from mathlib's quality).

is it in scope for me to PR a bunch of proof_wanteds to have these agents fill them in?

It is out of scope. Lean Pool only accepts complete formalizations of known mathematics. Your agent is as good as mine, so you can just give your proof_wanted to Claude/codex and PR the result to Lean Pool.

I used to moderate a low traffic category (a few submissions a day), which amounted to five minutes look at the end of a workday, but to the best of my knowledge the guys at CS.AI is a well organized team that take shifts on a strict schedule to cope with the flow.

I am not familiar with either of the two projects you mentioned. My goal is to be like arXiv. Serious Lean formalizations should be able to be disseminated quickly, and depended on in the long term.

Michael Rothgang said:

What kind of additional deterministic linters do you run? Can or should some of these become mathlib linters?

E.g. Lean Pool does not allow set_option, nolints, or warnings
There is a proof length linter (200 LOC is the current limit) and file length (at most 10k LOC).
There is also a linter for no sorry or axiom, etc. Lean Pool also does not currently allow native_decide. This is the CI description: link.

The only one that I can see being upstreamable is some measure of proof or decl length. Lean Pool's implementation is heuristic (just counting LOC, which can be cheated by cramming several tactics on one line) but a more robust implementation is possible e.g. with AST's. But IMO Lean Pool has to have stricter linters than mathlib because unlike mathlib it's not human reviewed.

Vasily Ilin said:

Michael Rothgang said:

What kind of additional deterministic linters do you run? Can or should some of these become mathlib linters?

E.g. Lean Pool does not allow set_option, nolints, or warnings
There is a proof length linter (200 LOC is the current limit) and file length (at most 10k LOC).
There is also a linter for no sorry or axiom, etc. Lean Pool also does not currently allow native_decide. This is the CI description: link.

Can you explain what these linters are supposed to guard against? Just general code quality or actually as a measure for cheating? I can name several ways to smuggle an axiom, sorry or native_decide into a file without mentioning any of them.

@Marcin Pilipczuk , right, I hope that the LLM reviewer can serve this role, at least partially. So far in my testing it works sufficiently well. For example this was correctly rejected as not significant and here the reviewer noticed lack of license, so the PR got rejected.

Btw, arXiv moderators have my sincere gratitude!

@Henrik Böving , these linters are supposed to help with code quality. For example, AI agents love to increase max heartbeats instead of decomposing, simplifying, and optimizing. They also love to make new axioms. And they love to just keep growing the proof into hundreds of LOC instead of making helper lemmas.

If your goal is to cheat, of course you'll find a way. Just like if your goal is to get a false mathematical result into arXiv, you will no doubt be able to do so. I don't see why anyone would intentionally do so - it will just hurt their reputation. That being said, I am curious to see some of your examples, as I am not an expert in Lean internals!

For the record: mathlib doesn't allow sorry, axioms or native_decide either (nor warnings), and also lints file length (so, you could use a mathlib linter for this!). Hard-disabling these is a change, but mostly that's enforcing mathlib's rules strictly.
The proof length linter could be useful. (I'd like to upstream a slightly different version: a long proof must have comments in between.) Would you be interested in adding that to mathlib?
99 messages were moved from this topic to #general > Discussion about OSS licenses for Lean projects by Johan Commelin.

Now that the (somewhat orthogonal) discussion about licensing was moved to another thread, I want to try to spark a discussion in what I view as the whole point of making Lean Pool.

I hope that people will start contributing to Lean Pool themselves instead of me importing projects. The only reason I pooled so many projects myself was for the proof of concept. I hope that Lean Pool becomes the place for individuals and AI companies to show off their latest finished formalization projects, in a way that can be reused by others.

My mental model for Lean Pool is similar to academia's arXiv and Isabelle's AFP. It's a place with minimal moderation and quality control, where people can collectively share their work and depend on each other's work, where their work is maintained, and where their work is searchable via the docs.

  1. [Add] If you have a formalization project that you won't upstream to mathlib, whether because of the AI policy or another reason, message me to add your project to Lean Pool, or just ask your own AI agent to make a PR for you using the instructions.
  2. [Use] If you are working on a formalization project, which depends on some mathematics that is not yet in mathlib, check if perhaps it is in Lean Pool, using the docs.

Let's pool our Lean together!
I'm really excited about "AFP for Lean"!

check if perhaps it is in Lean Pool, using the docs.**

Kim Morrison said:

I'm really excited about "AFP for Lean"!

Ironically "AFP for Isabelle" was one of the things which put me off Isabelle (what am I supposed to do if there are several choices for the definition of a ring?) so it's probably worth asking now if there are any plans about how to deal with this issue. Mathlib makes canonical choices for most mathematical objects but I am not convinced that this solves the problem because there are thousands of definitions which mathlib doesn't have. Here are two concrete things that can happen (and probably will happen if we're not careful).

1) Someone decides they don't like mathlib's definition of graph so just makes another one and pools it.
2) Two people read some random blog post by e.g. me saying "I need Hilbert modular forms to prove FLT" and both independently develop competing theories of Hilbert modular forms (e.g. someone has functions on the upper half plane, someone has the adelic version, and these definitions really do give different answers if the class group of the underlying totally real field is bigger than 1).

My impression with AFP is that all of this is fine and there are no guardrails at all. Is that also a viable plan here? One approach could be "let different definitions coexist and let natural selection decide". But I do think there is a certain amount of risk attached to this approach. Or perhaps by "risk" I mean "exciting new experiment".
If I had the money I'd just setup a bunch of AI maintainers who continually clean up the code people submit, as well as unifying and deduplicating work.

If not, I'll have to wait until PNT+ has upstreamed everything I need to mathlib.

Vasily Ilin said:

I hope that Lean Pool becomes the place for individuals and AI companies to show off their latest finished formalization projects, in a way that can be reused by others.

As I indicated in a message that got moved to the other thread despite not being about OSS licensing, I'd like us to make a lot more use of the mathlib archive (something between mathlib and Lean Pool) for finished projects. Appropriate principles for putting a finished formalization project in the mathlib archive might include:

  • Anything that could reasonably be a small lemma or piece of API in an existing part of mathlib proper should be factored out and go there, not in the mathlib archive (such small pieces can generally be PRed as you go along while working on a formalization project).
  • If more than one such finished project needs the same (larger) piece of mathematics, it should be factored out from those projects, digested and go in mathlib proper with appropriate generality and integration. But something only used in a single finished project might go directly in that project in the mathlib archive, in only the generality needed for that particular project, with full integration into mathlib being left until later or until another project needs the same mathematics.
  • The review process for someone making changes to their own project in the mathlib archive should be kept lightweight (though since it would be for finished projects, most of them probably wouldn't have many changes).
Sorry for moving all 99 messages in one go. I think the move is a net benefit, but I realize some messages got unfair treatment.

Let's pool our Lean together!

Could you clarify exactly what you will or will not accept in Lean Pool?
You said that adding incomplete projects such as proof_wanted/TODOs is out of scope, and that complete formalization projects are okay.

  • Should every PR be thousands of lines? (since it should be a complete project)
  • Should only LLMs contribute?

My mental model for Lean Pool is similar to academia's arXiv and Isabelle's AFP. It's a place with minimal moderation and quality control, where people can collectively share their work and depend on each other's work, where their work is maintained, and where their work is searchable via the docs.

AFAIK Isabelle's AFP has quite strict moderation and quality control, or at least that's the impression I get from their guidelines. What specifically are Lean Pool's moderation agents checking and how does it compare to AFP?

Is it math only? CS? What about recreational stuff like the Lean elevator game or maze game?
Or OEIS sequences / IMO solutions / Erdős problems? (which aren't cleaned up enough to live in existing repos such as compfiles)

Thanks!

If I had the money I'd just setup a bunch of AI maintainers who continually clean up the code people submit, as well as unifying and deduplicating work.

@Chris Birkbeck , this kind of thing is much cheaper than you might imagine. Even one $200 Codex subscription is enough to almost never run out of usage. IMO the bottleneck is what it means to "clean up" code. I have tried to distill the wisdom of mathlib maintainers into a doc that can be given to the cleaning-up agent, but I wouldn't call it successful.

If you have a script or prompt that works, I can cover the costs myself (again, it's not much), just let me know!

@Kevin Buzzard , thank you very much for the great question. This is one of the big concerns I have about Lean Pool as well. First, let me say that I don't have answers but I have ideas and the enthusiasm to try them out.

  1. Deal with it the same way that informal math deals with it: a mix of natural selection and just living with the duplicates (e.g. to some people compact means what others call pre-compact).
  2. Use LLMs to identify duplicates and unify them. I have already tried it on Lean Pool and the AI agent did not find any major duplicates. This can even be part of the CI. In fact, I already tried using LeanExplore to check for duplicates against mathlib but turned it off for now.

The first time a big duplicate happens will set a precedent. We will think about it, form a policy (e.g. having an AI attempt to unify the definitions) and follow the policy from there on.

So I think cleaning up code means getting it as close as possible to mathlib standards. Note that this is often harder than proving the result, I know this from my own work but we also saw this in sphere packing, where it was cheaper to prove the results than to do the initial round of cleaning. I've subsequently cut down the work by Math. Inc's Gauss by 50% by using a custom Claude skill which definitely does not produce mathlib quality code, but cleans up most of the easy things that AI loves to do. You can probably use this to make equivalent codex skills, but I would run /overview to keep track globally of what you have, then /cleanup and /cleanup-all regularly as well as /generalize to try and keep things manageable. I do this across my repos currently but it eats up my Claude credits very quickly.

@Fernando Portela , yes, and I even ended up contributing (in a small way) to PNT+ because of this. Since Lean Pool does not allow sorrys or axioms outside of the 3 standard ones, it will just have to wait.

@Snir Broshi ,

Should every PR be thousands of lines? (since it should be a complete project)

A complete project might be hundreds of lines. Lean Pool got its first community PR today (https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/pull/177), and it's 300 LOC.

Should only LLMs contribute?

Emphatically NO! I would love humans to contribute their projects - this is MUCH more valuable than AI projects, because human-authored projects tend to be of higher quality, and also human time and effort is infinitely more valuable than AI's time and effort. Most projects in Lean Pool are actually human-authored, at least as far as Claude can tell (it's not easy to tell).

If the code passes the reviewer agent will it get merged? Are there review rounds?

Not necessarily but very likely. I can see a couple reasons why it might not be merged despite passing the LLM reviewer: the profiler reports an egregious compilation time, or the LLM reviewer was somehow tricked or confused. But these are edge cases in my experience so far.

Is it math only? CS?

Any math and math-adjacent fields are fair game. Like arXiv.

What about recreational stuff like the Lean elevator game or maze game?

No, this is not in scope, because I don't think anyone would ever depend on that code. On the other hand, a game-theoretic formalization of some well-known game like Chess or Go is in scope. I expect that there won't be many such edge cases.

Or OEIS sequences / IMO solutions / Erdős problems?

If it's serious math that has been formalized without sorrys or axioms, it's in scope! Certainly OEIS, IMO and Erdos problems are serious math that others may want to build on top, so it's in scope!

What specifically are Lean Pool's moderation agents checking and how does it compare to AFP?

To see it at a glance, just look at any one PR, e.g. the latest merged one: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/pull/129. The GH actions are here. Here are the LLM reviewer instructions.

Hello! I was looking at lean pool, and I was wondering why you don't expose the various libraries in the lake file? They are presumably distinct, no?

How much sense does it make for Lean Pool to switch to an editorial model? Namely, a submitter submits an abstract and a repository fragment to one of a pool of editors; if the editor thinks it is worthy of consideration, they pass it on to the editorial board who do a quick evaluation. If the result is not interesting or the result looks too large or otherwise inappropriate for the pool, it gets returned and the editor says something like "Sorry, try another pool" or gives feedback or whatever is appropriate. If the editor says "Yes, we will consider it", the submitter then provides the full repository which is then automagically evaluated. If this fuller evaluation is passed, the submission is included with the proviso that if follow up evaluations reveal flaws, system abuses, or other no-nos, the submission is removed from the pool and the submitter is blacklisted from having any more submissions be considered.

This has the benefit (drawback?) of having some initial curation time by humans before a lot of entity time is spent processing a submission, as well as the benefit (drawback?) of revealing bad actors who are trying to mess up the pool. If a policy/format is set up for accepting abstracts and then submissions, one might get a high quality pool of mathematics comparable to and perhaps better than ArXiv.

Of course, if the idea is to let machines do all the work, then I am less sure of the relevance of Lean Pool to human generated mathematics.

@J. J. Issai (project started by GRP) , I don't quite understand how your procedure is different from opening a PR.
BTW, there are currently only 7 distinct human contributors to Lean Pool, and only one "editor". If Lean Pool receives a lot more submissions, we'll have to think about scaling up the infrastructure around it, but for now there are simply not enough submissions.
@Eric Wieser , I know we talked about the pros and cons but tbh I forgot at this point. I remember this design being more complicated, and I didn't fully understand what problem it solves.

The primary difference is that a PR contains a diff (or proposed diff) between how things are and how they should be. A submission to an editor contains an abstract and part of a diff, brief enough to be human reviewable quickly. The abstract is human-readable and contains a brief gist, and the partial diff backs up some of the gist. When this part looks like it might be accepted, then a full PR (or other form of full submission ) can proceed. The idea is to enable quick decisions and evaluation based on key parts of the proposal rather than a more complete evaluation which takes longer.
